Planning your support

Open the topics that matter to your team. These details explain how to prepare the work, review results and handle changes.

Notice where work keeps coming back.

Why this helps

A virtual assistant agency can start with a task your team already understands. Look for a recurring queue, a decision that waits for the same person every week, or a finished item that is hard to verify. These are three places to start.

Unanswered requests

A customer writes on two channels and receives two different answers. Start by bringing both requests into one record. Choose the person who owns the next reply, and agree what information they need before they can send it.

A calendar that keeps moving

Requests arrive faster than the executive can decide what matters. Start with a daily brief that separates routine scheduling from conflicts and decisions. Provide examples of meetings that can move and appointments that need explicit approval.

Work that is ready but still waiting

A page or campaign item has approved copy but no clear release owner. Define who checks the current version, who schedules it and where the final link is recorded. Move open questions into the review queue before they become last-minute delays.

See where the handoffs meet.

Why this helps

See how a virtual assistant agency can coordinate teams in this fictional example. They share one log and keep separate approval rules.

Morning: prioritise

Executive support checks the inbox and calendar. A prospect has requested an earlier demo, and a client meeting now overlaps with a deadline. The brief puts the conflict and proposed options in front of the calendar owner. The prospect’s request goes into the CRM queue.

Midday: handle and route

CRM support checks the prospect’s record and assigns a next action. A related support ticket asks for information the team cannot confirm yet. The assistant links the ticket and gives the product owner a clear decision to make before the customer receives another update.

Afternoon: release and record

Content support prepares an approved page for release. WordPress support checks the preview and records the published URL. The work log now shows the published page, the demo owner and the customer question still waiting for a decision.

Give your virtual assistant a clear starting point.

Why this helps

Use a fictional record if your example contains confidential information.

One normal example

Give your virtual assistant agency a request that usually goes well. Show the inputs, the decisions made and what the recipient expects at the end. If the output is a report, include the layout and what each field means.

One difficult example

Show a request that cannot follow the normal route. Explain what made it unusual, who decided what to do and how the decision was recorded. This helps define exceptions without writing instructions for every possibility.

A useful finish line

Choose the smallest outcome someone can verify. For an inbox brief that might be a list of decisions with deadlines. For a published page it might be a preview, approval and live link. Give the reviewer a way to say what needs to change.

Keep the record where the team looks for it.

Why this helps

A handoff can cross email, a help desk, a CRM or a publishing tool. Choose where the primary record lives and use links to carry context between tools. This keeps a status report from becoming a competing version of the work.

Pick the main record

Agree with your virtual assistant agency which system owns each field. A CRM might hold the contact and follow-up owner, while a help desk holds the conversation. Agree how to handle disagreement before copying an old value into a second place.

Scope the access

Give access to the specific tool and actions that the workflow needs. For a first publishing task, drafting and preview access may be enough. Let the relevant owner approve any additional rights.

Give decisions a route

A written rule should say who can approve an exception and where the response belongs. If an approver is away, the assistant needs a backup route and a way to show what remains blocked.

Check the work and improve the instructions.

Why this helps

A short review with your virtual assistant agency helps separate a poorly defined task from a mistake in the work. Start with a handful of real items and compare them with the result you agreed. Use what you learn to adjust the process before adding another queue.

Look at the output

Pick one completed item, one that needed a decision and one that is still open. Check whether the output is accurate, easy to use and stored in the right place. Review what would have made the open item easier to resolve.

Review the exceptions

Look for the same question coming up more than once. Decide whether the rule can be clarified, the task should stay with a specialist or the reviewer needs a better way to receive it.

Change one thing at a time

Write down the change and give the assistant an example. At the next review, check whether the change made the handoff easier. Keep any adjustment to permissions or coverage separate so it can be approved clearly.

Start at the level that fits your work.

Why this helps

Some teams need a single task taken off their plate. Others need coordination across a few queues. Ask your virtual assistant agency to start with work you can explain and review, then decide whether a wider scope makes sense.

One recurring task

Choose a daily or weekly item with a clear finish, such as an inbox brief or a content checklist. It is easier to learn the review process when the first task has familiar inputs and a named decision owner.

One complete queue

Define the types of requests that belong in the queue, the coverage window and the exceptions. Give the reviewer a sample of urgent and routine requests so they can see whether the queue rules are working.

A connected workflow

When several teams share a result, agree a handoff at each transition. A campaign brief can become a published page only after the asset, brand review and release approval are visible to the next owner.

Choosing the right support

Choose a useful first review

For the first review, pick a few ordinary tasks and one request that needed a decision. Look at what came back, whether the source was easy to find and how much explanation the reviewer needed. Give feedback about the result you want next time. A precise instruction, such as including the meeting time zone or linking the approved draft, is easier to apply than a general request to be more careful. Keep the improved example with the working instructions so the next task starts from the same understanding.

Plan a manageable working rhythm

Think about when the work arrives and when someone needs to act on it. A short daily update may suit a busy inbox, while a weekly review may suit research or publishing coordination. Explain which requests can wait and which should reach a named person promptly. If your priorities change, update the task list and the review schedule together. This helps your team understand the available support without treating every message as an urgent interruption. The right arrangement depends on the work you agree, rather than a promise of unlimited availability.

Frequently Asked Questions

What can I delegate?

Start with admin, customer enquiries, CRM updates, research or content coordination. The Services page has the full range.

Can I start with one task?

Yes. Agree one recurring task, the expected result and how you will review it.

Can you use my existing tools?

We plan the work around your approved tools and the access you authorise.

How will I get updates?

Agree an update schedule and a shared place for completed work, questions and next actions.

What access will you need?

Only the access agreed for the task. Decisions outside your instructions come back to your authorised reviewer.

How do I get started?

Contact our virtual assistant agency by email or phone with the task you want help with. We’ll discuss the scope and next steps.
